items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Eventually I wound up producing an album of him with Dave Holland. It was called For Evans Sake... I convinced him, 'Come on man! Stick it out!'... Dave goes and plays with Miles.

ctx.x: I did that one recording with Bill. “Live at Montreux.” Actually the best time I had with Bill was playing… …it’s a shame we didn’t record Bill at Ronnie Scott’s because we stayed at Ronnie’s for a month and it was nice because I actually got to see… …Philly Joe was living in London at the time so I got the chance to see Philly Joe quite a bit. Actually Joe sat in and I played some melodica with him and that’s also where I met some future Miles Davis friends. During the day I would go down to Ronnie’s and

Ronnie’s was open. The word went out that I wanted to come play with some of the British musicians, which for them was fantastic because a lot of the American musicians came and didn’t want to know anything about the British musicians. So Dave Holland, Jon McLaughlin, Pat Smythe. Another drummer, too, who actually plays with Cecil Taylor was Tony Oxley played drums because I was playing piano. I’d sit in and play piano. Then I’d play some drums, melodica. So we would be there jamming everyday. I really got to…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: And then we had Dave Holland, we had Colin Wolcott, what’s his name — Trilok Gurtu So there were a lot of current musicians that were like on the faculty teaching there.

ctx.x: You had an association with Karl Berger and the Creative Music Studio. Can you tell me how that came about and how you think about your contributions to that now, in retrospect? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

I think Karl Berger, I think Ornette has something to do with that. I just came and did some teaching with the students. And then we had Dave Holland, we had Colin Wolcott, what’s his name — Trilok Gurtu So there were a lot of current musicians that were like on the faculty teaching there. And so you know the challenge was for us, when we first started, was to play — to get the musicians who were at different levels of being able to play. Some couldn’t even play scales. Some — and so we had to try to figure out a…

He said an interesting thing that, he said, “Playing free requires more discipline, more stringent than anybody can tell me from the outside. The more precise you get, the more free you are.” And I remember when he said that I just like — wow — that if you observe it and listen to it you may get the impression that people are just playing randomly and that’s not what he’s about at all.
